title: Type Systems
tagline: Static vs dynamic, strong vs weak, type inference, generics, and soundness — the rules that govern what a value is allowed to do.

sections.content:
Every value in a program has a **type** — a description of what it is and what operations are valid on it. You can call `.toUpperCase()` on a string but not on a number. You can multiply two floats but adding a boolean to an object is at best ambiguous, and at worst a silent bug. A **type system** is the formal machinery that tracks these descriptions throughout your code and uses them to prevent or detect errors.

Type systems are one of the most consequential design decisions a language makes. They determine what kinds of bugs you catch before shipping, how much annotation ceremony you endure while writing code, how expressive your abstractions can be, and how fast your tools can help you navigate and refactor a codebase. The difference between a JavaScript codebase riddled with `undefined is not a function` errors and a TypeScript codebase where those errors surface as red squiggles before you even run the code — that difference is the type system at work.

Type systems live across several independent axes. The **static vs dynamic** axis determines *when* type checking happens — at compile time or at runtime as the program runs. The **strong vs weak** axis determines *how strictly* the runtime or compiler rejects implicit type conversions. **Type inference** is the compiler's ability to deduce types from context without requiring you to annotate every variable. **Generics** (also called parametric polymorphism) let you write one function or container that works safely with many different types. And **soundness** describes whether a type system can be trusted completely — whether it guarantees that a well-typed program will never produce a type error at runtime.

This chapter unpacks each of these dimensions in depth: what they mean, how they work mechanically, where they came from historically, how they interact with each other, and what the tradeoffs are. Understanding type systems is not just academic — it shapes how you read compiler errors, how you design APIs, and how you reason about correctness in any language you use.

sections.caption: The four main dimensions of a type system. Static/dynamic and strong/weak are independent axes — a language can be any combination of the two.

sections.title: The Warehouse Inspector
sections.content:
Imagine a warehouse where every box has a label describing its contents: *books*, *electronics*, *fragile glassware*. A **static type system** is like an inspector stationed at the loading dock who reads every label before a single box is moved. She refuses to load a crate labelled *fragile glassware* onto the same pallet as boxes labelled *heavy machinery*. If a forklift arrives with an unlabelled box, she sends it back immediately — she will not let anything leave without a verified label. Problems are caught before departure. **Nothing ships with a type error.**

A **dynamic type system** is like a warehouse that skips the label check at the dock. Boxes go out freely. But when the delivery truck arrives at the destination and the recipient opens the crate expecting books and finds a chainsaw, *that is when the error surfaces* — at runtime, in production, possibly in front of your customers.

**Strong typing** means the inspector is ruthless about mismatches even within the warehouse. She will not quietly move a chainsaw into a books box even if the forklift operator insists it will probably fit. **Weak typing** means the warehouse is relaxed: if the chainsaw technically fits in the box, it goes in — chaos at the destination is someone else's problem.

**Type inference** is the smart inspector who can deduce what a box contains from its weight, shape, and smell without requiring a written label. You still get safety without the annotation overhead. And **generics** are like stackable containers designed to hold *any* type of contents safely — the container enforces that whatever goes in also comes out with the same label, regardless of whether that label says books or electronics.

sections.title: Static vs Dynamic Typing: When Are Types Checked?
sections.content:
**Static typing** means the type checker — whether a compiler or a standalone tool — analyses the program *before execution*. It assigns a type to every expression and verifies that every operation is valid for the types involved. If you write `const x: number = 'hello'`, a static type checker refuses to proceed. You fix the error before the program ever runs.

Languages with static type systems include TypeScript, Java, C#, Rust, Go, C++, Haskell, and Kotlin. The benefits are substantial: errors are caught at the earliest possible moment, IDEs can provide precise autocomplete and refactoring because they know the exact type of every identifier, and the type annotations serve as machine-checked documentation that can never drift out of sync with the implementation.

**Dynamic typing** means types are attached to **values**, not variables. A variable is just a name that can point to any value at any time. When you write `let x = 42; x = 'hello'; x = [1, 2, 3];` in JavaScript, all three assignments are valid — `x` simply holds whatever value you put in it. Type errors are only discovered at runtime, when an operation is attempted on a value whose type does not support it: `null.length` throws a `TypeError` the moment the line executes.

Languages with dynamic type systems include JavaScript, Python, Ruby, PHP, Lisp, and Erlang. The benefits here are different: faster prototyping (no annotation overhead), maximum flexibility for metaprogramming and reflection, and natural support for heterogeneous data where the same variable genuinely needs to hold different types across its lifetime.

**The performance implication**: Because a static type checker resolves types before execution, the runtime does not need to carry type tags alongside every value. A Java `int` is just 32 bits in memory with no tag. In a dynamic language like Python, every integer is a full object with a type pointer, reference count, and the actual value — significantly more memory and slower access. This is one reason statically typed languages often outperform dynamic ones for compute-intensive work.

**A nuance**: TypeScript deserves special mention. It is statically typed *at development time*, but types are erased before runtime — the output is plain JavaScript. There is no runtime type enforcement from TypeScript itself. This makes TypeScript a **compile-time type system** in the strictest sense.

sections.title: Strong vs Weak Typing: How Strictly Are Mismatches Handled?
sections.content:
The **strong vs weak** axis is orthogonal to static vs dynamic — it describes *how aggressively* the language rejects or allows implicit type conversions (coercions) when a type mismatch occurs.

**Strongly typed** languages reject type mismatches rather than silently converting one type to another. In Python, `'3' + 3` immediately raises a `TypeError: can only concatenate str (not 'int') to str`. Python is dynamically typed but strongly typed — the error surfaces at runtime, but it surfaces immediately and clearly, not silently producing a wrong result.

**Weakly typed** languages (sometimes called loosely typed) will implicitly convert values to make an operation work. JavaScript is the canonical example. `'3' + 3` evaluates to `'33'` because JavaScript coerces the number to a string. But `'3' - 1` evaluates to `2` because the minus operator has no string version, so JavaScript coerces the string to a number. `[] == false` evaluates to `true` through a six-step abstract equality algorithm involving two separate coercions. These coercions are not bugs in JavaScript per se — they are intentional design decisions — but they produce counterintuitive results that become a fertile source of defects.

C is **statically typed but weakly typed**: the compiler assigns types to declarations, but it freely allows casting a pointer of one type to a pointer of another type. This is the foundation of both C's power (direct memory manipulation) and its danger (buffer overflows, use-after-free, undefined behaviour from strict aliasing violations).

Rust is **statically typed and strongly typed**: the compiler assigns types at compile time and provides essentially no implicit conversions. You must call `.to_string()` explicitly, use `as` casts that are well-defined and bounded, or implement `From`/`Into` traits. This verbosity is a deliberate choice that makes Rust programs far easier to reason about.

**The key insight**: *static/dynamic tells you when; strong/weak tells you how strictly.* They are independent. Python is dynamic+strong; JavaScript is dynamic+weak; Rust is static+strong; C is static+weak; TypeScript is static (mostly) and moderately strong (with `any` weakening it).

flowchart LR
  A["Static + Strong\nRust, Haskell, Java"] --- B["Static + Weak\nC, C++ (with casts)"]
  C["Dynamic + Strong\nPython, Ruby"] --- D["Dynamic + Weak\nJavaScript, PHP"]
  A --- C
  B --- D
sections.caption: The two axes form a 2x2 matrix. Most modern languages aim for the static+strong quadrant. C deliberately occupies static+weak for low-level systems access.

sections.title: Type Inference: Safety Without Verbosity
sections.content:
Early statically typed languages required the programmer to annotate every variable: `int x = 0; String name = "Alice"; List<Integer> nums = new ArrayList<Integer>();`. This verbosity was a legitimate criticism — dynamic language fans pointed out that annotating the obvious felt like busywork.

Type inference answers that criticism: **let the compiler figure out the type from context, so you only annotate where it is genuinely ambiguous or important as documentation.**

`const x = 42` — TypeScript infers `x: number`. `const greeting = 'hello'` — TypeScript infers `string`. `const nums = [1, 2, 3]` — TypeScript infers `number[]`. You get static-typing safety without any annotation overhead for simple, obvious cases.

**Local type inference** (TypeScript, C# `var`, Java `var`) works within a single expression or statement. The compiler looks at the right-hand side of an assignment and deduces the type. This covers the vast majority of everyday code.

**Global type inference** (Hindley-Milner algorithm, used in Haskell, OCaml, Elm, early Rust) can infer types across an entire program without any annotations at all. The Hindley-Milner algorithm works by generating type constraints from every usage of a value and then solving the constraint system simultaneously. In Haskell, you can write a complete program with no type annotations and the compiler will figure out all types — yet the type system is one of the most rigorous in existence.

**Where inference breaks down**: inference cannot always work. When a function is called from multiple places with different argument types, or when a generic type parameter needs to be explicitly locked down, you need an annotation. This is why TypeScript requires you to annotate function parameters in many cases even though it infers return types. A good rule of thumb: *annotate function signatures (they are your API contract), let inference handle local variables.*

**Type widening**: TypeScript sometimes infers a type wider than you want. `const x = 'north'` gives `x: string`, but you might want the narrower literal type `'north'`. Use `const x = 'north' as const` or an explicit annotation `const x: 'north' = 'north'` to keep the narrower type. Understanding widening helps you use inference precisely.

sections.title: Generics: One Implementation, Many Types
sections.content:
Suppose you want to write a function that returns the first element of an array. Without generics, you have two bad options: write a separate function for each element type (`firstNumber`, `firstString`, `firstUser`), or use a single function that takes and returns `any` — losing all type safety.

Generics solve this cleanly. A **type parameter** (written `<T>`) is a placeholder that gets resolved at each call site:

```typescript
function first<T>(arr: T[]): T {
  if (arr.length === 0) throw new Error('Empty array');
  return arr[0];
}
```

When you call `first([1, 2, 3])`, TypeScript infers `T = number` and the return type is `number`. When you call `first(['a', 'b'])`, `T = string`. The compiler verifies correctness at each call site without you having to duplicate the implementation.

**Constraints** restrict which types are valid for a type parameter. `T extends { length: number }` means T must have a `length` property — strings, arrays, and custom objects qualify, but plain numbers do not. This lets you call `x.length` inside the function body without losing the ability to pass different types.

**Generic data structures** are where generics shine most. `Array<T>`, `Map<K, V>`, `Set<T>`, `Promise<T>` — these container types are useful for any element type. Without generics you either write separate `NumberArray`, `StringArray` etc. (code explosion) or you use a single untyped container that loses all type information.

**Multiple type parameters**: `function zip<A, B>(as: A[], bs: B[]): [A, B][]` takes two type parameters. The function pairs elements from two arrays into tuples, and the compiler correctly types the output based on the input types.

**Variance** is an advanced topic that arises with generics: is `Array<Dog>` a subtype of `Array<Animal>`? Covariant means yes (safe for read-only containers), contravariant means `Array<Animal>` is a subtype of `Array<Dog>` (safe for write-only containers), invariant means neither direction is safe (necessary for mutable containers). TypeScript handles variance through structural subtyping, which is pragmatic but occasionally unsound.

**Historical context**: Generics were introduced to Java in 2004 with Java 5 (after the language launched in 1995 without them). Before Java 5, all collections were `Collection<Object>` and you cast on retrieval — runtime `ClassCastException` errors were common. Java generics are implemented via **erasure**: the type parameter is checked at compile time and then erased from the bytecode, so `List<String>` and `List<Integer>` are the same class at runtime. C++ templates, by contrast, generate separate code for each instantiation — more powerful and faster, but with longer compile times and larger binaries.

sections.label: Example
sections.explanation: JavaScript demonstrates both dynamic typing (variables hold any type) and weak typing (silent coercions). The `strictAdd` function simulates Python-style strong typing by throwing on mismatched types. The generic `getLength` pattern shows what the TypeScript constraint `T extends { length: number }` does at runtime — it enforces that the value has a numeric `.length` property, covering strings, arrays, and compatible custom objects.

sections.title: Nominal vs Structural Typing: What Makes Two Types Compatible?
sections.content:
Once you have a type system, a crucial question arises: when is a value of type A acceptable where type B is expected? There are two major schools of thought.

**Nominal typing** (also called name-based typing) says two types are compatible only if they are explicitly declared to be related. In Java, if you have class `Dog` and class `Cat`, both with `{ name: string; speak(): string }`, a `Cat` cannot be used where a `Dog` is expected — even though they have identical shapes. Compatibility comes from explicit `extends` or `implements` declarations, not from coincidental structural similarity.

**Structural typing** (also called duck typing in its dynamic form, and shape-based typing statically) says two types are compatible if they have the same *structure* — the same fields and methods with compatible types — regardless of what they are named or where they were declared. TypeScript uses structural typing: if an object has a `name: string` and a `speak(): string` method, it satisfies an interface declaring those, whether or not it explicitly implements that interface.

**TypeScript's structural approach** is pragmatic for JavaScript interoperability. Because JavaScript objects are created ad-hoc without class declarations, TypeScript cannot require explicit type relationships. If a function expects `{ name: string }` and you pass `{ name: 'Alice', age: 30 }`, TypeScript accepts it because the object has all the required fields (and more). This is called *excess property tolerance* for non-literal types.

**Nominal typing's advantage** is explicitness. In a large codebase, two types that happen to have the same fields might mean very different things semantically — a `UserId: string` and an `AccountId: string` should not be silently interchangeable even if they are both strings. Nominal typing enforces this distinction by name. Some TypeScript patterns simulate nominal typing using **branded types**: `type UserId = string & { _brand: 'UserId' }` — an intersection that adds a phantom property to create a distinct type name without changing the runtime representation.

**Duck typing** is the dynamic-language equivalent of structural typing: if it walks like a duck and quacks like a duck, treat it as a duck. Python's protocol system (`typing.Protocol`) is a formally specified form of structural typing for static analysis tools like mypy.

sections.title: Soundness, Unsoundness, and the Practical Tradeoff
sections.content:
A type system is called **sound** if it provides a guarantee: *if a program passes the type checker, it will never produce a type error at runtime.* Soundness is the gold standard of type safety. Languages that achieve it include Haskell, OCaml, Elm, and Rust (for safe code). In these languages, if it compiles, it will not crash with a type error.

Achieving full soundness requires restricting certain convenient features. Haskell has no `null` — absence is encoded explicitly as `Maybe a`. Rust has no null pointers and no implicit coercions. Elm makes it essentially impossible to write a program that throws a runtime exception.

**TypeScript is intentionally unsound.** The design team made a deliberate choice: TypeScript will not sacrifice pragmatic JavaScript interoperability for theoretical soundness. Several features break soundness:

- **`any`**: A value typed `any` opts out of the type checker entirely. You can call any method on it, pass it anywhere, and no compile error occurs — but runtime errors can still happen.
- **Type assertions** (`as Type`): You can override the compiler's judgment entirely. `(value as string).toUpperCase()` — if `value` is not actually a string at runtime, you get a runtime error despite the type assertion.
- **Covariant arrays**: TypeScript allows `string[]` to be used where `object[]` is expected, which is technically unsound (you could push a number into what the string array code thought was a string array).
- **`as unknown as T`** double casting: Lets you lie to the compiler completely — `const x = 0 as unknown as string` — a common workaround for testing code.

**The practical result** is that TypeScript catches the vast majority of real-world type errors — studies suggest 15–38% of all JavaScript bugs can be detected statically by TypeScript — while remaining usable for existing JavaScript codebases. Unsoundness is concentrated in explicit escape hatches (`any`, `as`) that developers consciously choose to use.

**`unknown` vs `any`**: TypeScript offers `unknown` as a sound alternative to `any`. A value typed `unknown` can be assigned from anything, but you cannot use it without first narrowing it through a type guard. This gives you the flexibility of accepting any value as input while maintaining safety in how you use it.

flowchart TD
  A["Value typed 'any'"] --> B["Type checker skips it"]
  B --> C["No compile error"]
  C --> D["Possible runtime TypeError"]
  E["Value typed 'unknown'"] --> F["Must narrow first"]
  F --> G["typeof check\nor instanceof check"]
  G --> H["Narrowed to specific type"]
  H --> I["Safe to use — compile verified"]
sections.caption: The difference between 'any' and 'unknown' in TypeScript. 'any' is an escape hatch that removes type safety; 'unknown' forces you to prove the type before using the value.

sections.label: Example
sections.explanation: Structural typing checks shape — the `greet` function accepts any object with a `name: string` field, regardless of class declaration. Union types and narrowing let a value be `string | number` while the compiler tracks which branch applies to which type. Branded types simulate nominal typing in TypeScript by adding a phantom property that makes two otherwise identical string types incompatible.

sections.title: Type Guards, Narrowing, and Discriminated Unions
A Brief History: How Type Systems Evolved
sections.content:
The study of type systems in programming languages has deep roots in mathematical logic. Bertrand Russell's **type theory** (1908) was developed to resolve paradoxes in naive set theory. Alonzo Church's **typed lambda calculus** (1940) gave a formal foundation for reasoning about programs with types. These theoretical developments eventually influenced programming language design.

Early compiled languages like **FORTRAN** (1957) and **COBOL** (1959) had primitive type systems — mainly distinguishing integers from floating-point numbers to ensure correct arithmetic operations. **ALGOL 60** introduced block-structured types. **Simula** (1967) and **Smalltalk** (1972) introduced classes and object-oriented type hierarchies.

The landmark theoretical development was the **Hindley-Milner type inference algorithm**, developed independently by Roger Hindley (1969) and Robin Milner (1978). It proved that types in a functional program could be inferred completely and uniquely without any programmer annotations. This result was implemented in the **ML** language family (ML 1973, Standard ML 1983, OCaml 1996) and later Haskell (1990). These languages demonstrated that you could have a powerful, expressive, fully inferred static type system.

Mainstream adoption came later. **Java** (1995) brought static typing to the masses but required verbose annotations. **Generics** were added to Java in 2004 and to C# earlier in 2005. **Go** (2009) adopted static typing with inference but deliberately kept the type system simple — no generics until 2022. **TypeScript** (2012) brought static typing to JavaScript through gradual typing and structural subtyping, finding a pragmatic middle ground.

The most recent developments explore **dependent types** (types that can depend on values — Idris, Agda, Lean), **refinement types** (types annotated with predicates — Liquid Haskell), and **gradual typing** (allowing static and dynamic regions to coexist in the same program — TypeScript, Python type hints, Typed Racket). The field continues to evolve, pushing the boundary of what properties compilers can verify automatically.

**Gradual typing** is a middle path between fully static and fully dynamic: you can annotate some parts of the codebase and leave others unannotated. TypeScript, Python's type hint system (with mypy), and PHP's type declarations all support gradual typing. The key property is that unannotated code is treated as `any` — it passes type checks without constraint but provides no guarantees. Gradual typing lets teams migrate incrementally from a dynamic to a static codebase, which is why TypeScript adoption has been so practical for large JavaScript projects.

**Common interview traps and misconceptions to know cold:**

- **'Statically typed = safe'** is false. C is statically typed but has no memory safety guarantees and allows any pointer cast. Safety requires strong typing AND memory safety (Rust provides both).
- **'Dynamically typed = slow'** is a generalisation. Modern JIT compilers (V8 for JS, PyPy for Python) use runtime type information to optimise dynamic code aggressively. The gap has narrowed but static typing still gives better worst-case performance for compute-intensive work.
- **TypeScript `any` vs `unknown`**: Know this cold. `any` opts out of type checking; `unknown` requires you to narrow before use. Prefer `unknown` for inputs of indeterminate type.
- **Type erasure in Java**: Java generics exist only at compile time. At runtime, `List<String>` and `List<Integer>` are both just `List`. This is why you cannot do `instanceof List<String>` in Java — the runtime has no knowledge of the type parameter.
- **Structural vs nominal**: TypeScript is structural (shape matters); Java and Go are nominal (declared relationships matter). Knowing this explains why `{ name: string }` in TypeScript is assignable from any object with a `name: string` field, even without explicit interface implementation.

items: **Static typing** checks types at compile time before the program runs, enabling early error detection and rich IDE tooling; **dynamic typing** checks types at runtime when operations are performed, enabling flexibility and faster prototyping.

**Strong vs weak typing is orthogonal to static vs dynamic**: Python is dynamic and strongly typed (rejects implicit coercions); C is static and weakly typed (allows unsafe pointer casts); Rust is static and strongly typed; JavaScript is dynamic and weakly typed.

**Type inference** lets the compiler deduce types from context — `const x = 42` gives `x: number` without annotation — providing static safety without verbose annotation overhead; Hindley-Milner inference can infer types across entire programs.

**Generics** (parametric polymorphism) use type parameters like `<T>` to write one function or data structure that works safely for many types; constraints like `T extends { length: number }` restrict which types are valid without giving up generality.

**Structural typing** (TypeScript, Go interfaces) makes types compatible by shape — matching fields and methods — while **nominal typing** (Java, C#) requires explicit declared relationships; structural typing is more flexible but can accidentally accept semantically incompatible values.

**Soundness** means a program that passes the type checker can never produce a runtime type error; TypeScript is intentionally unsound via `any` and type assertions for JavaScript interop pragmatism; prefer `unknown` over `any` to retain safety.

**Discriminated unions** (tagged unions) combine union types with a literal `kind` field to give the compiler enough information to narrow types exhaustively in switch/case patterns — a type-safe, functional-programming-derived alternative to nullable fields and `any`.

quiz.question: What is the fundamental difference between static and dynamic typing?
options: Static typing only supports primitive types; dynamic typing supports objects and functions.
Static typing verifies types at compile time before execution; dynamic typing attaches types to values and verifies at runtime when operations are attempted.
Static typing is used only in compiled languages; dynamic typing is used only in interpreted languages.
Dynamic typing requires explicit type annotations on every variable; static typing uses inference exclusively.
quiz.explanation: Static typing catches type errors before the program runs — at compile or type-check time. Dynamic typing defers type checking to runtime, discovering errors only when an invalid operation is actually attempted on a value. The distinction is about *when*, not about which types are permitted.

quiz.question: JavaScript evaluates `'3' - 1` as `2` (a number). This behaviour is an example of:
options: Strong typing — the runtime selects the most specific valid type.
Static type inference resolving the expression at compile time.
Weak typing — implicit coercion of the string '3' to the number 3 to make the operation work.
A runtime TypeError — JavaScript should throw here.
quiz.explanation: JavaScript is weakly typed: when the minus operator has no string version, it implicitly coerces '3' to the number 3 and performs arithmetic. A strongly typed language like Python would raise a TypeError at this point instead of silently converting.

quiz.question: Python raises `TypeError` when you write `'3' + 3`. What does this tell you about Python's type system?
options: Python is statically typed — it checks types at compile time.
Python is dynamically typed and strongly typed — types are checked at runtime but mismatches are rejected rather than coerced.
Python is dynamically typed and weakly typed — it coerces when possible and throws only when coercion is impossible.
Python uses nominal typing and therefore rejects this because str and int have different names.
quiz.explanation: Python is dynamic (types are on values, checked at runtime, not compile time) and strong (it rejects implicit coercions — adding a string and an integer is an error, not a silent conversion). This demonstrates that dynamic and strong are independent axes.

quiz.question: What problem do generics (parametric polymorphism) solve?
options: They allow runtime type checking to be skipped entirely for better performance.
They let a single function or class work correctly and safely for many types by introducing a type parameter resolved at each call site.
They convert dynamic type information into static annotations automatically.
They replace all runtime exceptions with compile-time type errors.
quiz.explanation: Without generics, you either duplicate code for each type or use an untyped container and lose type safety. Generics introduce a type parameter T resolved at each call site — `first<T>(arr: T[]): T` works for any element type while the compiler verifies correctness at every call.

quiz.question: What is Hindley-Milner type inference notable for?
options: It requires every variable to be explicitly annotated but then verifies the annotations are consistent.
It can infer types for an entire program without any programmer annotations, used in languages like Haskell and ML.
It is a runtime algorithm that attaches types to values as they are created.
It is a technique for erasing generic type parameters from bytecode at compile time.
quiz.explanation: Hindley-Milner generates type constraints from every usage of a value and solves the constraint system globally. The result is complete type inference across an entire program — Haskell programs can be written with no type annotations and the compiler will figure out all types correctly.

quiz.question: TypeScript uses structural typing. Which of the following best describes this?
options: A type is only compatible if it is explicitly declared to extend or implement the target type.
An object is compatible with a type if it has all the required fields and methods with compatible types, regardless of its declared class name.
Compatibility is determined by the file and directory structure of the project.
TypeScript converts all types to strings and compares them lexicographically.
quiz.explanation: Structural typing (duck typing) makes compatibility about shape — does the value have the required fields and methods? Java uses nominal typing (explicit declared relationships). TypeScript's structural approach is necessary because JavaScript objects are created ad-hoc without formal class declarations.

quiz.question: What does it mean for a type system to be 'sound'?
options: The type system can infer all types without any programmer annotations.
A program that passes the type checker is guaranteed to never produce a runtime type error.
The type system uses algebraic foundations based on sound mathematical logic.
The compiler emits warnings for every possibly unsound operation.
quiz.explanation: Soundness is the guarantee that a well-typed program cannot produce a type error at runtime. Haskell, OCaml, and Rust (safe code) achieve this. TypeScript is intentionally unsound — features like `any` and type assertions can allow runtime type errors that passed the type checker.

quiz.question: What is the key difference between TypeScript's `any` and `unknown` types?
options: `any` requires a type guard before use; `unknown` opts out of type checking.
`unknown` can only hold primitive types; `any` holds objects and functions.
`any` opts out of type checking entirely — you can do anything with it; `unknown` requires narrowing before use, preserving safety.
Both are identical at compile time; they only differ in how they are stored in memory.
quiz.explanation: A value typed `any` bypasses the type checker — you can call any method or assign it anywhere without error, but runtime errors can still occur. `unknown` accepts any value but forces you to narrow the type (via typeof, instanceof, or a type guard) before using it, maintaining type safety.

quiz.question: Java generics are implemented via type erasure. What does this mean?
options: Generic type parameters are inlined at compile time, generating separate classes for each type argument.
Generic types are checked at compile time but the type parameter information is removed from the bytecode, so `List<String>` and `List<Integer>` are the same class at runtime.
Type parameters are erased when the IDE encounters syntax errors, falling back to Object.
Erasure means generic types can only be used with primitive types in Java.
quiz.explanation: Java generics use erasure: the compiler checks type parameters and then removes them from the bytecode. At runtime, `List<String>` and `List<Integer>` are both just `List` — this is why you cannot do `instanceof List<String>` and why Java has unchecked cast warnings when mixing generics with legacy untyped collections.

quiz.question: A TypeScript function is declared as `function wrap<T>(value: T): { inner: T }`. What does TypeScript infer for T when called as `wrap('hello')`?
options: `any` — TypeScript cannot infer T without an explicit type argument.
`object` — TypeScript widens string literals to their base type.
`string` — TypeScript infers T from the argument type, so the return type is `{ inner: string }`.
`unknown` — TypeScript uses `unknown` for all inferred generic parameters by default.
quiz.explanation: TypeScript infers T = string from the argument 'hello'. The return type becomes `{ inner: string }`. Type inference resolves the type parameter at the call site from the argument's type, giving full type safety without requiring an explicit type argument like `wrap<string>('hello')`.
